sentences.text: Genyornis newtoni was a massive flightless bird that stood over two meters tall, with some estimates placing its height at 2.5 meters and its weight between 200 and 240 kilograms.
Its closest living relatives are ducks and geese, and recent studies found that it possessed a goose-like bill topped with a raised triangular casque.
The unique shape of its beak suggests it functioned as a combination of predator and scavenger.
Fossils of Genyornis have been found in articulation, a state not yet discovered in any other dromornithid species.
Eggshell fragments from around 200 sites show burn marks, suggesting humans collected and cooked Genyornis eggs.
Archaeologists found a rock painting possibly 40,000 years old that depicts two Genyornis individuals.
The original specimen, a left femur, was found at Lake Callabonna in South Australia.
Gastroliths, or stomach stones, have been found with Genyornis remains, indicating the fossils were often found in shallow sites.
Genyornis individuals at Lake Callabonna showed signs of osteomyelitis, likely caused by getting stuck in drying mud.
The genus Genyornis belongs to the family Dromornithidae, which existed in Australia for over 30 million years. Genyornis was the last known member of this extinct family.
The genus lived from the Gelasian to the Late Pleistocene, between 2.58 and 0.0117 million years ago. Genyornis newtoni was a flightless bird that lived in Australia until 50,000 years ago.
Genyornis fossils have been found in South Australia and New South Wales dating to the Pleistocene Epoch.

It is debated whether the eggshells with burn marks belonged to Genyornis or the extinct giant malleefowl. A 2022 study using protein sequences concluded the eggshells likely belonged to Genyornis, supporting earlier implications.
It is debated whether the rock art depicts Genyornis, as some studies suggest the art is only 14,000 years old and indistinguishable from other birds.

There is an ongoing debate between human impact and changing climate as the primary causes of Genyornis extinction. A 2024 study suggests Genyornis had adaptations for feeding on aquatic plants, tying them closely to freshwater habitats. It is debated whether Genyornis extinction was caused by their reliance on freshwater habitats that dried up during late Pleistocene aridification.
